title: Take Out the Gland, Put Back the Signal
endLine: Remove the source, replace the signal, show what travels in blood.

scenes.tts: How can an organ change the whole body without its own nerves? In 1849, a Göttingen physician put a testis back into the belly of castrated young cockerels. Even cut off from its original nerves, that organ let the birds grow combs and crow.
scenes.caption: How can an organ change the whole body without its own nerves? In 1849, a Göttingen physician put a testis back into the belly of castrated young cockerels. Even cut off from its original nerves, that organ let the birds grow combs and crow.
scenes.visual: Schematic body loop filling most of the frame height: a glowing source organ on the left (labeled 'Testis') connects to a target on the right (labeled 'Comb') via a blue nerve line above and a crimson bloodstream loop below. As the opening question plays, the nerve line snips and fades while the testis moves to the belly beside the blood loop; simple glowing dots drift through the blood to the comb, which grows larger next to a question mark. Marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: How can an organ change the whole body without its own nerves? In 1849, a Göttingen physician put a testis back into the belly of castrated young cockerels. Even cut off from its original nerves, that organ let the birds grow combs and crow.

scenes.visual: Over the gently flowing schematic bloodstream loop (dimmed slightly), the title 'Take Out the Gland, Put Back the Signal' fades in at high contrast, holds, and fades out.

scenes.tts: To find a chemical signal, you first take its source away. Removing a gland, or disabling it with a lesion, is called extirpation. Once secretion stops, normal clearance drains the blood level down, and the target response falls. Removal shows need, yet surgery might also cut nerves.
scenes.caption: To find a chemical signal, you first take its source away. Removing a gland, or disabling it with a lesion, is called extirpation. Once secretion stops, normal clearance drains the blood level down, and the target response falls. Removal shows need, yet surgery might also cut nerves.
scenes.visual: Same carried schematic body loop. The source organ on the left lifts off and vanishes before the label 'Extirpation' appears. Secretion halts while a small clearance drain arrow empties glowing droplets from the bloodstream; on the right, the target response gauge drops flat. A brief spark breaks along the blue nerve line to show surgery could also cut nerves. Marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: To find a chemical signal, you first take its source away. Removing a gland, or disabling it with a lesion, is called extirpation. Once secretion stops, normal clearance drains the blood level down, and the target response falls. Removal shows need, yet surgery might also cut nerves.

scenes.tts: To rule out cut nerves, you next test replacement. Place the organ in a new spot, or deliver the missing hormone directly. Droplets refill the blood, and the target response recovers. If function returns without original nerves, a chemical carries the signal.
scenes.caption: To rule out cut nerves, you next test replacement. Place the organ in a new spot, or deliver the missing hormone directly. Droplets refill the blood, and the target response recovers. If function returns without original nerves, a chemical carries the signal.
scenes.visual: Same carried schematic body loop with the blue nerve line still severed. The source organ reappears at a new site on the blood loop before the label 'Replacement' fades in, then transforms into a simple schematic pump feeding glowing droplets directly into the stream. As droplets circulate, the target gauge on the right climbs back to full height while the nerve path stays broken. Marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: To rule out cut nerves, you next test replacement. Place the organ in a new spot, or deliver the missing hormone directly. Droplets refill the blood, and the target response recovers. If function returns without original nerves, a chemical carries the signal.

scenes.tts: To test blood transport directly, experimenters use parabiosis, joining two animals' circulations. In joined mice, blood-borne factors cross while each nervous system stays separate. Here is the core rule. Remove the source to test need, replace the signal to restore function, and join bloodstreams to test transport.
scenes.caption: To test blood transport directly, experimenters use parabiosis, joining two animals' circulations. In joined mice, blood-borne factors cross while each nervous system stays separate. scenes.visual: The carried schematic body loop rises slightly as a second identical body loop slides in beneath it. Two crimson vessel bridges join their bloodstreams (labeled 'Parabiosis' once linked) while their blue nerve lines remain separate. Glowing schematic droplets cross from the top loop into the lower partner, lifting the partner's target gauge. Three compact step markers ('Remove', 'Replace', 'Share blood') light up in order along the bottom. Marked 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Yet replacement is not always as simple as adding hormone back. In rhesus monkeys, hypothalamic lesions cut off gonadotropin-releasing hormone, called G n R H. A pump replaces it as hourly bursts, or as a steady drip giving at least as much. Which schedule restores the pituitary's release of its two reproductive hormones?
scenes.caption: Yet replacement is not always as simple as adding hormone back. In rhesus monkeys, hypothalamic lesions cut off gonadotropin-releasing hormone, called GnRH. A pump replaces it as hourly bursts, or as a steady drip giving at least as much. Which schedule restores the pituitary's release of its two reproductive hormones?
scenes.visual: The second loop fades out and the single carried schematic loop returns to center, relabeled 'Hypothalamus' (dimmed by a lesion on the left) and 'Pituitary' (target on the right). A schematic pump joins the bloodstream and splits into two parallel feed tracks: top track pulses discrete packets ('Hourly bursts'); bottom track pours a continuous stream at equal or greater total volume ('Steady drip'). A question mark pulses over the pituitary readout. Marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Yet replacement is not always as simple as adding hormone back. In rhesus monkeys, hypothalamic lesions cut off gonadotropin-releasing hormone, called GnRH. A pump replaces it as hourly bursts, or as a steady drip giving at least as much. Which schedule restores the pituitary's release of its two reproductive hormones?

scenes.visual: Holds the carried rhesus-monkey schematic loop with both pump tracks gently pulsing droplets and the question 'Which schedule restores pituitary release?' displayed in large high-contrast text. Marked 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Only the hourly bursts restore luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. The steady drip shuts pituitary release down. The drip ran at four rates. The two highest gave as much hormone as the pulses, or more. So dose cannot explain the failure. The usual answer is desensitization: constant hormone makes pituitary cells turn their response down.
scenes.caption: Only the hourly bursts restore luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. The steady drip shuts pituitary release down. The drip ran at four rates. scenes.visual: On the same split-track schematic loop, the top hourly-burst track turns the pituitary gauge bright green and emits two labeled streams ('LH' and 'FSH'). On the bottom steady-drip track, a schematic dial steps through four flow rates, with the highest two matching or exceeding the burst dose, with a tag 'Not too little hormone', yet the pituitary gauge sinks flat and dims under the label 'Desensitization'. Marked 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Replacement also fails when a hormone is not missing. Fat cells make leptin, a fuel gauge reporting stored energy. Leptin replacement worked in o b o b mice, which lack leptin, and in rare people unable to make it. Most people with common obesity have high leptin, so replacement does not reliably help.
scenes.caption: Replacement also fails when a hormone is not missing. Fat cells make leptin, a fuel gauge reporting stored energy. Leptin replacement worked in ob/ob mice, which lack leptin, and in rare people unable to make it. Most people with common obesity have high leptin, so replacement does not reliably help.
scenes.visual: The carried schematic loop relabels the source 'Fat cells' sending 'Leptin' droplets to a brain gauge on the right. First, an empty vessel ('No leptin') receives pump droplets and the target gauge swings cleanly. Next, the same vessel fills thickly with circulating droplets ('High leptin'); extra pump droplets enter the crowded stream, yet the target gauge barely moves. Marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Replacement also fails when a hormone is not missing. Fat cells make leptin, a fuel gauge reporting stored energy. Leptin replacement worked in ob/ob mice, which lack leptin, and in rare people unable to make it. Most people with common obesity have high leptin, so replacement does not reliably help.

scenes.tts: In 1849, relocating a testis in castrated cockerels showed an organ can act without original nerves. In rhesus monkeys, pulsed G n R H replacement showed that signal timing matters. Medicine uses that rule. Leuprolide, a slow-release G n R H relative, stays steady, so the pituitary quiets and testosterone falls in prostate cancer.
scenes.caption: In 1849, relocating a testis in castrated cockerels showed an organ can act without original nerves. In rhesus monkeys, pulsed GnRH replacement showed that signal timing matters. Medicine uses that rule. Leuprolide, a slow-release GnRH relative, stays steady, so the pituitary quiets and testosterone falls in prostate cancer.
scenes.visual: Inside the carried crimson bloodstream frame, two schematic views build in sequence: first, the belly-placed testis driving comb growth with severed nerves (tagged '1849'); then a steady slow-release leuprolide stream (a flat, constant level, unlike the hourly bursts) quieting the pituitary gauge so a schematic testosterone bar drops (tagged 'Slow-release leuprolide'). Marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: In 1849, relocating a testis in castrated cockerels showed an organ can act without original nerves. In rhesus monkeys, pulsed GnRH replacement showed that signal timing matters. Medicine uses that rule. Leuprolide, a slow-release GnRH relative, stays steady, so the pituitary quiets and testosterone falls in prostate cancer.

scenes.tts: In 1996, Ahima and colleagues showed falling leptin in fasting mice helps set off the starvation response. Because leptin tracks stored energy, its drop signals low fuel. Take away the source, restore the pattern, and shared blood reveals what steers the body.
scenes.caption: In 1996, Ahima and colleagues showed falling leptin in fasting mice helps set off the starvation response. Because leptin tracks stored energy, its drop signals low fuel. Take away the source, restore the pattern, and shared blood reveals what steers the body.
scenes.visual: In the carried vessel frame, the fat-cell-to-brain loop drains as schematic leptin droplets thin out during fasting, swinging a schematic fuel-gauge needle into a starvation-response zone (tagged 'Ahima and colleagues, 1996'). The vessel then widens back to the clean full-frame loop with source, bloodstream, and target glowing in unison. Marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: In 1996, Ahima and colleagues showed falling leptin in fasting mice helps set off the starvation response. Because leptin tracks stored energy, its drop signals low fuel. Take away the source, restore the pattern, and shared blood reveals what steers the body.

scenes.visual: The carried schematic bloodstream loop softens into the background while the end card displays centered, high-contrast type: 'Remove the source, replace the signal, show what travels in blood.'
